html:
In October 2026 Google Research released harness2, the code behind the paper Harness²: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World. A harness is everything around a model that lets it act as an agent: the system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts and plugins. harness2 improves that harness one task at a time without touching the model's weights. For each task it proposes edits, probes them by running the task again, and composes a refined harness from how the runs behaved differently. A second, slower loop keeps an improvement harness with the harnesses it adopted and the lessons it drew, and uses them on the next task. On three professional benchmarks the authors report that a single step improves two models over their base harnesses: by up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench and 11.8 percentage points on LAB's partial pass rate.

It is a research framework, and it feels like one. You install it into a Python 3.12 virtualenv, export a handful of environment variables, start a long run by hand, watch it scroll and then read the results as files: one directory per task, eight harness components per candidate, rollouts, trajectories and judge verdicts. That works for one researcher at one terminal. It does not work when several people share a machine, when the run spends real money on cloud models, or when you want an AI coding agent to start and analyse sweeps without handing it a shell.

Harness² Workbench is what I designed and shipped around it: an unofficial, Apache-2.0 GUI, REST API and MCP server that drives harness2 through its own command line and reads what it writes. It does not modify harness2, and it is not affiliated with Google; the method and its credit belong to the paper's authors. Version 0.1.0 is pinned to, and tested against, harness2 commit 1cfe254.

This post is the overview: what the Workbench does, how it is put together, and where its limits are. The other posts in the series go deep on the MCP server, the two security reviews, the supply-chain rules, four flaky tests and taking the repository public.

What it does

Every harness2 operation becomes a job: installing harness2 at the tested commit, the free offline demo, benchmark setup and readiness checks, dry-run previews, refinement sweeps in either recursion mode with every flag, judging, reports, train/test splits, multi-step pipelines and the Codex bridge. Jobs queue, stream their logs live, can be cancelled, stop on a timeout, and a run can carry an optional spend limit.

Everything harness2 writes can be browsed instead of opened by hand: the tasks of a sweep with their scores, the harness tree of every candidate (the eight components, from c1 system prompt to c8 plugins), the diff between the base harness and the one harness2 adopted, the rollouts and their trajectories, the experience library the improver builds, the improver's own audit trail, and reports. Two results can be compared task by task with a sign test that says, in plain words, whether a difference is more than chance. An adopted harness can be exported as raw files or as an OpenCode or Codex project, ready to use outside harness2.

Around that sit the things a shared tool needs: API tokens with three roles (viewer, operator, admin), browser sessions and single sign-on behind a trusted proxy; write-only secrets with best-effort redaction from logs; model profiles for Vertex AI and OpenAI-compatible endpoints; a cost estimate before a run; an environment doctor that names the fix for each problem it finds; a hash-chained audit log; Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry traces; and a guided tour for someone who has never heard of harness2.

How it is built

The Workbench is a Rust workspace of six crates: h2w-api (the wire types), h2w-core (the domain logic: harness2's command lines, its file layouts, the results readers), h2w-daemon (the server), h2w-web (the UI, compiled to WebAssembly), h2w-mcp (the MCP server) and an end-to-end test crate, plus a mock API for UI work and a build tool. Eight architecture decision records explain the choices; the ones that shaped everything else:

  • Wrap the CLI, never import the Python. harness2 has no library API; its command line and its on-disk layout are its contract. Running it as a separate process, with an explicit argument vector and no shell, keeps its crashes out of the server and lets an existing checkout keep working unchanged.
  • One server owns everything. Jobs, state, authentication, roles and the audit log live in one process. The MCP server is a thin client that forwards the caller's token to the REST API, so an agent never has more than the rights of its token, and roles, limits and the audit log live in one place.
  • SQLite for state, plain directories for results. A single-node tool does not need Postgres. Each experiment is an ordinary harness2 run directory, so harness2's own tools still work on it.
  • One language end to end. The UI is Leptos, rendered in the browser and compiled to WebAssembly, sharing its types with the server. It loads under a strict Content-Security-Policy with no inline script or style at all, because this is an admin page that can start processes.
  • Two isolation modes. host, the default, runs executors the way upstream does, as the server's own user, and a host-mode run or pipeline has to acknowledge that risk explicitly; container runs each step in a hardened runner image whose only way out is an allowlisting egress proxy.

The interfaces were written down before any of the implementation: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md is a build contract with the wire types locked, and apart from the project's own rename before its first push, every later change to it was additive and versioned (four addenda, v1.1 to v1.4). The REST API is generated from those types as an OpenAPI 3.1 document with 49 operations, and the MCP server exposes 42 tools on top of it.

Running jobs safely

A harness2 sweep starts executors (OpenCode or Codex) that read and write files, call models and run code. The job engine treats that seriously:

  • Every step gets its own process group, so a cancel reaches everything the step started: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period.
  • Restart recovery identifies before it signals. If the server crashes with jobs running, the next start fails those jobs and stops their processes, but only after a positive identification: the same boot, the recorded leader's start time, and a H2W_JOB_ID marker that every step carries in its environment. A process group that cannot be identified is left alone. One CI run caught that check misreading a process in the middle of an exec; the flaky-tests post tells that story.
  • Limits are on by default: a cap on each job's stored log (256 MiB), a free-disk floor that stops running jobs and a timeout. A run or pipeline can also carry a budget; its guard watches the improver spend harness2 records (executor spend is not recorded there, which the model guide says).
  • Container isolation runs each step with every Linux capability dropped, no-new-privileges, a process limit and an internal network, as the server's own unprivileged user (on a rootless runtime that is container root, which maps to it). Job variables reach the container through a 0600 environment file, not through the container runtime's own environment. The egress proxy allows only listed hostnames and ports: an IP literal never matches, and a name that resolves to a private address is refused unless its entry allows it.

The honest part is written into the README in bold: host isolation is not a sandbox. An executor in host mode runs as the Workbench's own user, so a malicious or prompt-injected one can read the Workbench's database and rewrite its files. It is, in effect, an administrator. Container isolation exists for exactly that reason, and the docs say which mode each deployment gives you.

Reading what a job wrote, without trusting it

Everything a job writes is untrusted: a prompt-injected executor controls the files the Workbench later reads to show results. Two independent security reviews spent much of their effort here, and the security post has the details. The result is a reader that opens files without following symlinks and without blocking (a FIFO swapped in for summary.json used to hang a worker thread forever), refuses anything over its size cap, charges every request against a budget of bytes and sweeps, stops when the client goes away, and caps a response at 64 MiB and a log page at about 1 MiB.

The interface

The web UI is a single-page application that the server embeds and serves itself. It has a dashboard, an experiment and sweep browser, a task view with harness trees, diffs, rollouts and exports, a run wizard with a cost estimate, live job pages, the comparison view, settings for profiles, secrets, tokens and the audit log, a command palette and keyboard shortcuts, a dark theme and a phone layout. Each role sees only what it may use, and the docs list which pages were exercised against a real server and which only against the mock API.

What is proven, and what is not

The README's feature matrix gives every feature two labels: whether it is implemented, and whether it was verified live, covered by tests with fakes only, or unverified. That table is the most useful thing in the repository, because it is also the most honest:

  • 641 unit and integration tests and 7 end-to-end tests run on every push. The end-to-end suite starts the real server and the real harness2 demo, drives the UI in headless Firefox and runs the demo through an MCP client.
  • The REST API, sign-in, most of the job engine, container isolation, the egress proxy, the MCP server and most of the UI were verified live against a real server and the free demo. Cancelling a running job, the timeout and the budget guard are covered by tests with stand-ins only.
  • No model-backed sweep has been run through the Workbench. The only real harness2 workflow exercised end to end is the offline demo. Benchmark sweeps are parsed against recorded harness2 output, and WorkBuddy-Bench is partial because upstream supports it only on Vertex AI.
  • Two independent security reviews found 27 issues between them, and a final documentation pass found three more in the code. Each one was fixed, or narrowed and recorded in the threat model as a residual risk. No human penetration test has been done.

The documentation runs to about 72,000 words: a user guide with screenshots, an administrator's guide with the full configuration reference, REST API and MCP guides, a model-profile guide, a STRIDE threat model, troubleshooting indexed by exact error message, the eight decision records and a supply-chain policy. A link checker fails the build on any broken relative link or anchor.

Shipping it

Version 0.1.0 came out on 24 October 2026. The release workflow built archives for x86_64 and aarch64 Linux with checksums, a CycloneDX SBOM, GitHub build-provenance attestations and the licence texts of every crate compiled in, as a draft. It was published only after a downloaded archive matched its checksum and the binary ran the demo. A runner image and an all-in-one image build from the repository, and a reference Compose deployment puts the Workbench on an internal network with the egress proxy and TLS in front.

What I would do next is the obvious gap: run real, model-backed sweeps through it on each benchmark and turn the "fakes only" rows of the feature matrix into "verified live". The rest of the series covers what it took to get here:

  • An MCP server for an agent harness that will not let a model accept risk for you
  • Two security reviews of a localhost control plane
  • A 14-day dependency cooldown, and three ways Dependabot slipped past it
  • Four flaky tests a fast machine hid
  • Taking a repository public: the checklist I actually ran
